summary: Describes the Wireless LAN Control Protocol, a proposal for central control and provisioning of large-scale wireless LANs, aimed at the CAPWAP objectives. This is a historic document, and it was replaced by RFC 5415.

eli5.summary: This is another early plan for letting one central computer manage many wifi boxes in a big network. A later standard replaced it.

questions: how does wicop manage wifi networks
subtitle: A protocol for central management of large-scale wireless LANs.

tldr.problem: Large wireless networks need central management, but different manufacturers use different control systems. There is no standard way for a central controller to manage access points from multiple vendors.
tldr.mechanism: WiCoP uses a common header and control packet format that identifies the wireless architecture in use (Local MAC or Split MAC). Devices exchange capabilities, establish security, receive configuration, and report status through a series of message types.
tldr.outcome: WiCoP was another early proposal in the CAPWAP standardization process. It was superseded by RFC 5415, which became the IETF standard.

today: RFC 5414 is Historic. It was replaced by RFC 5415, which became the IETF standards-track CAPWAP solution. WiCoP should not be used as the basis for any Internet deployment.

sections.title: Wireless LAN Control and Architectures
sections.content:
Wireless LAN deployments have grown large and complex, with hundreds or thousands of access points covering entire organizations. Managing these individually is impractical. WiCoP (Wireless LAN Control Protocol) enables a single Access Controller (AC) to centrally manage many Wireless Termination Points (WTPs).

The protocol recognizes that wireless networks use different internal architectures. In Local MAC architecture, each WTP performs all 802.11 medium access control functions and bridges traffic to the wired network. In Split MAC architecture, some functions are split between the WTP and AC, with the WTP handling low-level radio functions and the AC handling higher-level management. WiCoP accommodates both approaches in a single framework.
sections.eli5: Wifi networks can be organized two main ways inside: one way has each wifi box do its own thing and talk to a central boss (Local MAC). The other way splits the jobs between the wifi box and the boss (Split MAC). WiCoP handles both.

sections.title: State Machine and Operational Phases
sections.content:
WiCoP defines five operational states for both WTPs and ACs. In Initialization, devices power on and reset. In Capabilities Exchange, the WTP discovers the AC and both sides identify each other's capabilities. The Connection state establishes a secure channel between them. During Configuration, the AC sends long-term settings to the WTP. In the Operation state, they exchange ongoing status updates, statistics, and management instructions.

WiCoP makes an important design choice: it uses separate tunnels for different types of traffic. A control tunnel carries WiCoP management messages. Separate tunnels carry data traffic for each logical group (such as each virtual access point). This separation allows fine-grained control and policy for shared WLAN infrastructure.
sections.eli5: Wifi boxes go through five stages: waking up, saying hello, shaking hands, getting instructions, then working. WiCoP keeps control messages separate from data, and keeps each wifi network's data separate too.

sections.title: WiCoP Packet Structure
sections.content:
WiCoP packets have a common header used for both control and data packets. The header includes a version field, a MAC-type field ('M') that identifies whether the WTP is Local MAC (value 1) or Split MAC (value 0), and a differentiator field ('D') that specifies sub-variants. Other header bits indicate whether the packet is control ('C' field), whether it is retransmitted ('R' field), and whether it is encrypted ('E' field).

Control packets add a second header with a message type field (24 message types are defined), a sequence number for pairing requests and responses, and a message element length field. Message elements (TLVs) carry specific data such as WTP manufacturer ID, capabilities, configuration data, encryption settings, statistics, and error information. Each message element type has its own set of information items with defined lengths and formats.
sections.eli5: Every WiCoP message starts with a header saying what kind of box it is and what kind of message it is. Control messages add more headers describing what the message is about. Then specific information items fill the message, each with a type and value.

sections.title: Capabilities Exchange and Configuration
sections.content:
When a WTP enters Capabilities Exchange, it sends information about itself: manufacturer ID, MAC address, firmware version, and its 802.11e and 802.11i capabilities. The AC responds with information about its own capabilities and the control architecture it supports.

During Configuration, the AC sends configuration parameters per ESSID or per logical group. These include physical layer settings (power level, channel, operating mode), encryption type and keys, beacon interval, DTIM period, data rates, and QoS parameters. The AC can also configure virtual access points (multiple logical networks on one physical WTP) by sending configuration data indexed by BSSID.

WiCoP also supports shared infrastructure WLANs with multiple logical groups. The AC maintains logical group tunnels in addition to control tunnels. Each logical group can have independent configuration for encryption, QoS, and policy, even though they share a single physical WTP.
sections.eli5: First, the wifi box tells the boss what it can do. Then the boss tells it exactly what to do: what channel, what wifi names to broadcast, what passwords, and how to handle each customer's network separately if there are multiple logical groups.

sections.title: Operation, Updates, and Management
sections.content:
Once configured, WTPs and the AC enter Operation state. WTPs send periodic feedback messages containing statistics: transmission attempts, receive errors, beacon and probe counts, and encryption failures. The AC uses these statistics to monitor network health and adjust configuration as needed.

The AC can push configuration updates to WTPs during Operation. It can also trigger firmware downloads using TFTP data in WiCoP messages. WiCoP supports terminal management in Local MAC mode (WTP reports when stations associate and disassociate) and in Split MAC mode (AC sends terminal information to WTP). Key configuration messages allow updating encryption keys for wireless terminals. WiCoP also defines keepalive messages and error notifications to maintain the session and report problems with wireless interfaces or flash memory.
sections.eli5: While working, the wifi box sends regular reports to the boss: how many things got sent, how many had errors, and so on. The boss can update the wifi box's settings anytime, push new firmware, and both watch for problems and fix them.
